filt_text: With a 1% filter and iterative scans off, the HNSW scan returned 0.38 rows on average instead of 10 (68% of queries returned nothing; recall 0.04). strict_order returned 10.00 rows at recall 0.935 in 22.7 ms; relaxed_order 10.00 rows at recall 0.975 in 15.6 ms; the B-tree pre-filter with exact search was always right (recall 1.000) in 6.6 ms. With a 10% filter and iterative scans off, the HNSW scan returned 3.97 rows on average instead of 10 (1% of queries returned nothing; recall 0.40). strict_order returned 10.00 rows at recall 0.961 in 1.6 ms; relaxed_order 10.00 rows at recall 0.979 in 1.6 ms; the B-tree pre-filter with exact search was always right (recall 1.000) in 154.0 ms. Iterative scans fix the empty results; the price is latency and, at the 1% filter, the 20,000-tuple scan limit. Pre-filtering wins when the filter is selective, because exact search over about 5,230 rows is cheap; at 10% it must compute about 52,300 distances per query.
hyb_text: On Quora, vectors beat BM25 (nDCG@10 0.839 against 0.733) and fusion landed between them (0.825). On SciFact, BM25 beat vectors (nDCG@10 0.686 against 0.645) and fusion beat both (0.714). Per question on Quora, BM25 was better on 150, vectors on 388, and they tied on 462: the two retrievers fail on different questions, which is what fusion exploits when both are comparably strong (SciFact) and why an equal-weight fusion costs a little when one is much stronger (Quora). Requiring every word (fts_and) or ranking without idf (fts_or) costs the most; the HNSW index (ef_search 100) gave up little against exact vector search.
